analysis.one_liner: Lets big media companies own more TV stations, newspapers, and radio outlets in the same markets.
analysis.headline: The bill got no cosponsors, never left a House subcommittee, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have told the Federal Communications Commission to loosen its media ownership rules: ending the ban on one company owning both a newspaper and a broadcast station in the same city, raising the national cap on TV audience reach from 39% to 45%, discounting UHF stations when calculating that cap, and letting a single company own two TV stations in the same market if enough other stations remained. The result would have been more consolidation of local news and information under fewer, larger companies. The bill was introduced by one representative with no cosponsors and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Large broadcast station groups and newspaper chains, which could combine print and broadcast outlets in the same market, buy more stations nationwide, and own two stations in a single city. Consolidated owners gain more bargaining power over advertisers and more control over what local audiences see and hear.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the FCC rule limiting broadcast licenses to parties that own a daily newspaper, allowing newspaper publishers and broadcasters to own each other in the same market [S2][S3].
Raises the national audience reach cap for TV stations owned by one entity from 39 percent to 45 percent of TV households, letting the largest station groups grow bigger [S2][S3].
Counts UHF stations as reaching only 50 percent of a market's TV households when calculating the national cap, making it easier for owners to add UHF stations without hitting the limit [S2][S3].
Lets one company own two TV stations in the same market if their coverage areas do not overlap, or if at least six independent broadcast or cable TV voices remain in the area [S2][S3].
Ordered the FCC to make all of these changes within 90 days of enactment, overriding the commission's own ongoing review of its ownership rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Local audiences, who would have fewer independent owners of local news and public affairs programming, since communities across the country would see print and broadcast outlets fall under common ownership. Smaller and independent station owners would also face stronger competitors and fewer chances to sell stations at a premium.
analysis.who_pays_short: Local viewers and independent station owners

drawbacks.text: The bill's 'independent voices' test counts all cable television in a market as just one voice regardless of how many channels it carries, which inflates the appearance of local diversity while cable's local-news offerings are often shared across markets [S3].

Newspaper-broadcast combinations let one company own the main daily paper, a TV station, and radio stations in the same town, concentrating local news coverage in a single owner's hands — an outcome FCC cross-ownership rules had long restricted [S2][S3].
Raising the national reach cap to 45 percent lets the largest networks reach nearly half the country's TV households, reducing the number of voices in national news coverage [S2].
The bill ordered the FCC to act within 90 days, short-circuiting the case-by-case review of local market conditions that ownership rules normally involve [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go to a narrow set of large media companies, while the costs — fewer independent local voices, less diverse news coverage — are spread across everyone who relies on local news. The bill offered nothing to the public in return; its entire substance is the removal of ownership limits. The one honest argument for it, that consolidation can help struggling local stations survive, is not addressed anywhere in the bill itself.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Telecommunications subcommittee, where it stayed with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Cliff Stearns introduced the bill on April 13, 2005 [S1][S5].

The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and on April 22, 2005 to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet — where the action record ends [S5].
No further action was taken before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, so the bill died in subcommittee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Local news viewers and independent station owners are better off, because the existing limits on newspaper-broadcast combinations and national TV reach stayed in place. Large broadcast and newspaper companies lost their chance to consolidate further.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Local viewers and independent station owners

for.name: Rep. Cliff Stearns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to loosen media ownership rules; it drew no cosponsors

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Telecommunications subcommittee and never held a hearing or markup on it

sides.party_line_note: With a single sponsor and no cosponsors, no votes, and no floor action, there is no record showing a partisan split either way.

industries.industry: Large broadcast TV station groups and networks
industries.note: The bill raises the national audience cap to 45 percent, discounts UHF stations toward that cap, and allows two-station duopolies in the same market — directly expanding how big these companies can get. Their gain is the public's loss of independent local outlets.
Ending the newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership ban would let publishers buy or combine with radio and TV stations in their own markets. That concentrates local news in fewer hands.
The cross-ownership change opens radio licenses to newspaper owners, but the bill's main expansions concern TV, so radio's role here is secondary.

The bill counts the entire cable system in a market as one 'independent voice,' using cable's presence to justify allowing broadcast duopolies — a role cable had no say in and little to gain or lose from directly.
